## Option Pricing

A **derivative** or **contingent claim** has a **payoff** $h$ that depends on
the price process $(S_t)$ of an underlying asset, either at maturity,
$h(S_T)$, as for a [[european-options|European option]], or along the path,
$h(S_{[0,T]})$, as for an Asian option. See [[derivatives]] for the
definitions.

The key idea of pricing is the **principle of no arbitrage**, which states
that we cannot make a profit without risk. To determine the fair price of the
derivative we describe the dynamics of $(S_t)$ and compute the expected
payoff, adjusted for the time value of money and for risk. There are two
equivalent approaches, both developed below for the Black-Scholes-Merton
model:

- the **risk-neutral approach**, which prices the claim as a discounted
  expectation under a change of measure,
- the **PDE approach**, which prices the claim by replicating it with a
  self-financing portfolio.

## Black-Scholes-Merton Model

:::{.definition data-title="Black-Scholes-Merton Model"}

The Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) model considers a market consisting of two
assets: a risk-free asset (e.g. a bond) $(B_t)$ and a risky asset (e.g. a
stock) $(S_t)$, with dynamics given by [[geometric-brownian-motion]] (GBM)

$$
\begin{align}
dB_t & = rB_t\,dt, \tag{1}\\
dS_t & = \mu S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW_t, \tag{2}
\end{align}
$$

where $r$ is the risk-free interest rate and $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are the
**drift** and **diffusion** components of the
[[stochastic-calculus|stochastic differential equation (SDE)]].

:::

Equation $(1)$ is an [[ordinary-differential-equations|ODE]] with solution

$$
B_t = B_0 e^{rt}, \tag{3}
$$

and the solution to GBM $(2)$ is

$$
S_t = S_0 \exp\left( \left( \mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2} \right)t + \sigma W_t \right).
\tag{4}
$$

## Risk-Neutral Approach

Under the real-world measure $\mathbb{P}$, the drift $\mu$ of $(S_t)$ reflects
the preference of investors for larger returns on riskier assets. The
arbitrage-free price of a derivative is therefore not its discounted expected
payoff under $\mathbb{P}$, since buyers must be compensated for risk.

Instead we change to the risk-neutral measure $\mathbb{Q}$, constructed with
[[girsanov-theorem]], under which the discounted stock price $e^{-rt}S_t$ is a
[[martingale-theory|martingale]]. The drift of $(S_t)$ becomes $r$,

$$
dS_t = rS_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW_t^{\mathbb{Q}}, \tag{5}
$$

where $W^{\mathbb{Q}}$ is a Brownian motion under $\mathbb{Q}$. The
construction, the density $d\mathbb{Q}/d\mathbb{P}$ and the conditions for it
to exist are in [[risk-neutral-pricing]]. The price at time $0$ of a claim
with payoff $h(S_T)$ is the discounted expected payoff

$$
V_0 = e^{-rT}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[h(S_T)]. \tag{6}
$$

## PDE Approach

The idea is to build a self-financing replicating portfolio from the stock and
the bond that has exactly the same payoff as the claim. Assuming no arbitrage,
the portfolio and the claim must have the same price.

Let the portfolio hold $a_t$ units of stock and $b_t$ units of bond (with
$B_0=1$), so its value is $V_t = a_tS_t + b_te^{rt}$. Self-financing means
$dV_t = a_t\,dS_t + rb_te^{rt}\,dt$. Writing $V_t = u(t,S_t)$ and comparing
this with [[ito-formula]] applied to $u$ gives

$$
a_t = \partial_x u(t,S_t),
\qquad
b_te^{rt} = u(t,S_t) - S_t\,\partial_x u(t,S_t),
$$

and the function $u$ must solve the Black-Scholes PDE

$$
\partial_t u + rx\,\partial_x u + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2x^2\,\partial_{xx}u - ru = 0,
\qquad u(T,x) = h(x).
$$

The price of the claim at time $0$ is $V_0 = u(0,S_0)$. The full derivation by
delta-hedging, and an interpretation of the terms, is in
[[black-scholes-merton-model|the Black-Scholes PDE section]] of the
Black-Scholes-Merton note. By the [[feynman-kac-formula]], the solution of
this PDE is the risk-neutral expectation $(6)$, so the two approaches agree.
